article_title: An Evaluation of Teaching-Family (Achievement Place) Group Homes for Juvenile Offenders
author: Kathryn A. Kirigin; Curtis J. Braukmann; Jay D. Atwater; Montrose M. Wolf
community_group: Achievement Place; 12 Teaching-Family replications; 9 conventional Kansas group homes
page_locator: article pp. 1-16; especially method, Figures 1-2, Tables 2-5, and discussion
source_access: primary article full text and bibliographic record; DOI and PubMed/PMC record verified
evidence_type: nonrandom comparative residential-program evaluation using court and police records plus multi-party consumer ratings
exact_factual_observation: The study compared the original Achievement Place, 12 Teaching-Family replications, and nine conventional group homes. During treatment, Teaching-Family programs had lower alleged criminal-offense rates and a lower proportion of youths involved in alleged criminal offenses and received higher consumer ratings. There were no significant during-treatment differences for noncriminal offenses such as running away, truancy, and curfew violations. In the one-year post-treatment period, none of the reported between-program differences was statistically significant.
what_source_establishes: A family-style residential program with trained caregivers, explicit teaching, self-government, reinforcement, quality control, resident feedback, and conduct-record review can show better measured criminal-conduct outcomes during residence while failing to show a significant advantage after exit. During-residence and post-exit outcomes must be separate.
what_source_does_not_establish: The homes and youths were not randomly assigned; records were incomplete or inconsistently maintained; unmeasured selection and implementation differences remain; no single program element is isolated; victim outcomes and recurrence by conduct type are absent; and the study does not identify a persistently dangerous-child subgroup or authorize private communities to assume juvenile-placement or treatment powers.
author_interpretation: The authors conclude cautiously that Teaching-Family conditions appeared to reduce delinquent behavior during treatment more than comparison programs and discuss training and implementation quality as possible contributors.
alternative_interpretation: Selection, surveillance, record practice, local program quality, regression, or small post-treatment samples may explain part of the pattern. A later critical reanalysis disputes how strongly the null post-treatment result should be read, so the durable conclusion is the original study's reported lack of statistically significant post-treatment differences, not proof of no effect.
response_process: Court-adjudicated placement; residence in six-to-eight-youth group homes; trained teaching-parent interaction, reinforcement, self-government, skill teaching, school and family contact; police/court record review; consumer rating; one-year post-treatment check.
outcome: Measured criminal conduct and satisfaction favored Teaching-Family homes during treatment; noncriminal conduct did not; no reported outcome difference remained statistically significant one year after treatment.
transferability: High for separating behavior inside a dense residential structure from behavior after exit and for requiring transition and follow-up. Medium for the setting-level components. Low for direct transfer to intentional communities or the most severe persistent violence.
likely_article_destination: Community as therapist / child safeguarding / outcome dashboard / dangerous-child branch
notes: Adjacent residential/group-home evidence, not intentional-community evidence. Do not treat court involvement, a conviction, residence, compliance, or program completion as a danger or safety proxy.

track: Track D adjacent residential setting-level prevention
article_title: Intervening at the Setting Level to Prevent Behavioral Incidents in Residential Child Care: Efficacy of the CARE Program Model
author: Charles V. Izzo; Elliott G. Smith; Martha J. Holden; Catherine I. Norton; Michael A. Nunno; Deborah E. Sellers
community_group: 11 residential group-care agencies serving mostly child-welfare referrals
page_locator: article pp. 554-564; program description, methods, results, Figure 1, discussion, and conflict disclosure
source_access: open primary article full text; DOI, publisher, PubMed, and PMC records verified
evidence_type: staggered multiple-baseline interrupted time-series evaluation with 12 baseline and 36 implementation months
exact_factual_observation: Eleven agencies implemented six CARE principles through leadership and implementation teams, five-day manualized training, local trainers, quarterly consultation, observation, coaching, reflective practice, and organizational change. Relative to baseline trends, monthly incident rates declined significantly for aggression toward staff, property destruction, and running away. Results for aggression toward peers and self-harm were less consistent across cohorts. The authors disclosed program-development and evaluation roles.
what_source_establishes: Residential incidents are partly setting events: caregiver expectations and responses, relationships, routines, developmental fit, and the physical and social environment can affect escalation. A whole-setting intervention requires explicit principles, an implementation team, staff training, coaching, observation, and conduct-specific measurement.
what_source_does_not_establish: The design was not randomized; rising baseline trends, history, reporting changes, and agency differences may account for part of the result; incident reports are interaction and documentation measures as well as youth-behavior measures; there is no individual allegation, assessment, treatment, victim, recurrence, or post-exit sequence; and the study does not establish effectiveness in a lay-run intentional community.
author_interpretation: The authors interpret the findings as support for upstream setting-level prevention that reduces coercive caregiving patterns and creates healthier interactions.
alternative_interpretation: Staff may have de-escalated more effectively, reported differently, or both. Concurrent organizational change, regression from worsening baselines, or cohort-specific conditions may contribute. Fewer formal incidents do not by themselves prove better wellbeing or less unreported harm.
response_process: Agency-wide implementation team; six care principles; five-day training; quarterly technical assistance; observation and coaching; monthly incident reporting; statistical review of baseline-versus-implementation trends.
outcome: Aggression toward staff, property destruction, and running away declined relative to baseline trends; peer aggression and self-harm results were inconsistent; no post-exit outcome was measured.
transferability: Medium-high for designing a measured and developmentally informed residential setting function. Low for individual clinical response or direct intentional-community transfer. Independent safeguarding and clinical routes remain necessary.
likely_article_destination: Community as therapist / collective childrearing / outcome dashboard / dangerous-child branch
notes: Adjacent residential/group-care evidence. Report each harm category separately and disclose developer, funder, and evaluator roles.

track: Track E adjacent clinical and community child intervention
article_title: The Effectiveness of the Stop Now and Plan (SNAP) Program for Boys at Risk for Violence and Delinquency
author: Jeffrey D. Burke; Rolf Loeber
community_group: 252 boys aged 6-11 referred to two authorized community SNAP providers
page_locator: article pp. 242-253; sample, intervention, repeated outcomes, official records, and discussion
source_access: primary author manuscript and bibliographic record; DOI, PubMed, and PMC records verified
evidence_type: intent-to-treat randomized effectiveness trial with standard-services comparison and 3-, 9-, and 15-month measurement
exact_factual_observation: Families of 252 boys with clinically elevated aggressive, rule-breaking, or antisocial behavior were randomized to SNAP (130) or standard services (122). SNAP began with a three-month group component and could continue with individualized services throughout the 15-month study. SNAP produced greater reductions on several parent-rated aggression, conduct, externalizing, and symptom outcomes; the adjusted aggression effect was small (about d=0.29). Among 150 youths old enough for juvenile jurisdiction, the share with any new charge was lower but not significantly different, while the number of charges was significantly lower in SNAP. Some benefits persisted and others did not.
what_source_establishes: A structured response can combine conduct-specific intake, child problem-solving and emotion-regulation skills, caregiver involvement, continuing individualized support, fidelity oversight, repeated measurement, and official-record outcomes. Randomized comparison is more informative than communal reputation or uncontrolled persistence.
what_source_does_not_establish: The study does not concern residential or intentional-community governance; primary behavioral outcomes relied on parent report; the sample included boys only; recruitment and service-use selection remain; both groups could receive other services; rare justice outcomes were based on small counts; individualized SNAP services continued during follow-up; and the study does not establish results after all treatment stops or for children who remain gravely dangerous.
author_interpretation: The authors conclude that SNAP produced clinically meaningful reductions relative to standard services, may be especially helpful at higher initial severity, and may reduce charges.
alternative_interpretation: Differential service uptake, parent expectancy, additional services, selection among families willing to randomize, and continued intervention can explain part of the effect. Greater response at higher severity is not a validated danger or personality screen.
response_process: Clinical-threshold intake; random assignment; three-month child and caregiver group component; continuing individualized services as needed; fidelity assessment; repeated parent, symptom, service, and official-record measurement through 15 months.
outcome: Several behavioral and symptom differences favored SNAP through follow-up; some did not persist; any new justice contact was not significantly different, while charge counts were lower; follow-up overlapped continuing individualized treatment.
transferability: Medium-high for requiring child-plus-caregiver skill work, trained providers, individualized follow-on, fidelity review, and repeated outcomes. Low for peer-delivered treatment, residential transfer, or a lay community screening protocol.
likely_article_destination: Community as therapist / non-waivable child rights / collective childrearing / outcome dashboard / dangerous-child branch
notes: Adjacent clinical/community evidence, not intentional-community evidence. No retrospective diagnosis, lay assessment tool, compelled treatment, or membership sanction follows from this finding.
